newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: Bolivia says may have been hit by Mars probe.
newsitem.headline: Bolivia says may have been hit by Mars probe.

text.p: Bolivia said on Thursday the ill-fated Mars 96 space probe carrying lethal plutonium that was believed to have plunged in Chile may actually have fallen in its southern province of Oruro.
Environment Minister Moises Jarmusz told local television a study of possible impact sites showed the Russian satellite could have hit the Andean province on the border with Chile.
"This is like a science fiction movie," he said. "Thank God (Oruro) is a sparsely populated area. There are some communities of no more than 1,000 inhabitants that we must start to monitor."

Jarmusz said Bolivia has asked the United States to send experts to help it locate the craft carrying eight ounces (200 grams) of radioactive plutonium. The country has also been in contact with Chilean authorities, who have been conducting an intensive and so far fruitless search.
"We are concerned because if there are any people in the area the radiation can cause cancer, malformations. We are talking of a real hazard," Jarmusz said.
There have been no reports of any impact sightings. The craft re-entered the atmosphere on Nov. 16 and was widely believed to have plunged either in Chile or the Pacific.

Although most of the probe was thought to have burned on re-entry, the U.S. space agency NASA has said parts of it may have fallen in a large area of land and sea in northern Chile, which borders Oruro.
The incident has caused widespread safety concerns in Chile and friction with Moscow, which Santiago accuses of withholding information vital for finding the probe.

Russian officials reject the charges and say there is no danger of radioactive pollution because the plutonium is stored in containers designed to withstand the heat and stress of landing on Mars. The Mars 96 craft fell after takeoff when a booster rocket misfired, preventing it from breaking free of Earth's gravity.
